title: Set Work Study: John Williams – Main Title from Star Wars Episode IV: A New Hope
content_html:
The Symphonic Revival: Why Star Wars Sounded Like Old Hollywood

In 1977, mainstream film scoring had drifted towards pop songs, jazz-tinged underscoring and electronic textures, and full orchestral, wall-to-wall scoring was widely seen as old-fashioned. John Williams’ score for Star Wars: Episode IV – A New Hope, and above all its Main Title, reversed that trend almost overnight, reviving the grand symphonic sound of Hollywood’s golden age for a new generation of blockbuster film.

Director George Lucas asked Williams for a score that sounded grand, heroic and unmistakably melodic, closer to the adventure films of the 1930s than to contemporary science-fiction scoring. Williams responded with a set of recurring themes played by a full orchestra, opening the film with a brass fanfare so immediate and memorable that it quickly became one of the most recognisable pieces of orchestral music of the twentieth century, instantly signalling adventure before a single image has fully registered on screen.

The Main Title is written for full symphony orchestra and was recorded by the London Symphony Orchestra under Williams’ own direction, giving the cue the scale, precision and warmth of a concert-hall performance rather than a small studio ensemble.

Stylistic Ancestors: Korngold and Holst

Williams did not invent this symphonic film language from nothing. He drew directly on Erich Wolfgang Korngold, the Austrian-born composer whose lush, late-Romantic scores for 1930s and 1940s swashbuckling films, including The Adventures of Robin Hood, established the model of a large orchestra carrying the emotional and narrative weight of a film through memorable, singable themes and rich, chromatic harmony.

As you listen to Korngold’s title music, notice how brass fanfares announce heroism, strings surge beneath the melody, and the orchestration constantly shifts colour to match the action on screen; this is precisely the model Williams revived forty years later for a very different kind of adventure film.

A second, very different ancestor is Gustav Holst’s orchestral suite The Planets, particularly the movement Mars, the Bringer of War. Its relentless quintal harmony, driving irregular rhythm and enormous brass and percussion forces create a sense of mechanised menace that many listeners hear echoed in Williams’ scoring for the Empire and its forces later in the film.

Listen to how Holst layers ostinato patterns and builds tension through repetition and orchestral weight rather than melody alone; Williams borrows this technique of ostinato-driven tension for darker, more menacing cues elsewhere in the score, while keeping the Main Title itself bright, tuneful and optimistic by deliberate contrast.

The Fanfare Opening: Brass, Rising Intervals and Triplets

The Main Title begins with a bold unison fanfare, immediately establishing the heroic character before the main theme has even started. Horns and trumpets leap upward through rising fourths and fifths, wide, open intervals that project confidently and are easy for a listener to recall, which is exactly why they work so well as a recurring theme across a two-hour film.

Underneath the fanfare, Williams uses triplet figures, three even notes fitted into the space of two, to add rhythmic urgency and forward motion. These triplets appear both in the opening fanfare and later in the famous swashbuckling main theme, giving the music a sense of energetic momentum appropriate to a story about rebellion, escape and adventure across the galaxy.

The fanfare’s rising fourths and fifths are a deliberate compositional choice: these intervals sound bright and open rather than closed or resolved, which is why they instantly signal heroism and adventure to a listener before any narrative context has been given.

Leitmotif as the Score’s Engine

The single most important technique in the score is leitmotif, a recurring musical idea attached to a character, place or idea, a technique pioneered by Richard Wagner in his nineteenth-century operas. Williams builds almost the entire Star Wars score around a handful of these themes, of which the Main Title theme, sometimes called the hero’s theme, is the most important of all.

Because the Main Title theme returns throughout the film whenever heroism, adventure or the Rebellion is on screen, the opening fanfare functions as far more than an overture: it is the thematic engine that Williams reuses, transforms and develops across the whole film, giving over two hours of music a strong sense of musical unity and dramatic recognition for the audience.

As you watch the Main Title, follow the brass fanfare into the sweeping main theme played by full strings and horns ; listen for how the triplet rhythms and rising intervals from the opening return, varied but recognisable, and notice the sheer size and confidence of the orchestral sound Williams establishes within the first minute alone.

B flat Major, Orchestration and the Sound of Adventure

The Main Title is written in the bright, open key of B flat major, a key strongly associated in the brass and wind repertoire with confident, celebratory writing, because it sits comfortably within the natural range of trumpets and horns, allowing them to play with a full, ringing, resonant tone.

Williams scores for a full symphony orchestra: brass, including horns, trumpets, trombones and tuba, carry the main fanfare and theme; woodwind and strings add warmth and sweep beneath and around it; timpani and percussion reinforce the rhythm and add weight at climactic moments. This combination of a memorable tonal melody, full orchestral forces and clear, functional harmony is what creates the unmistakable sound of adventure that has come to define blockbuster film music ever since 1977.

The choice of B flat major, combined with rising fourths and fifths in the brass, is not decorative: both features make the fanfare physically easier and more resonant for brass instruments to project, which is part of why the theme sounds so triumphant and works so effectively in live concert performance.

Exam Focus: Listening for Construction

In your listening exam, you may be asked to identify features of the Main Title from a short extract, so practise recognising the fanfare’s rising fourths and fifths, the triplet rhythms, the key of B flat major, and the full orchestral texture, and be ready to explain why each feature creates a heroic, adventurous mood.

You should also be able to place the piece in context: a symphonic score written in 1977 that consciously revived the late-Romantic Hollywood style of Korngold and the powerful, driving orchestral writing of Holst, using Wagnerian leitmotif technique to unify an entire film through a small number of recurring, transformable themes.
exam_tip_html: When asked to explain rather than just identify a feature, use the pattern 'feature + technical cause + effect on listener': for example, do not simply write 'it uses a fanfare', write 'the rising fourths and fifths in the brass fanfare sit high in the natural range of the instruments, so the sound projects brightly, creating an immediate impression of heroism' — examiners reward the causal chain between the technical detail and the emotional or dramatic effect, not the label alone.
conclusion_html: You now know how Williams fused Korngold’s lush late-Romantic Hollywood style with Holst’s driving orchestral power and Wagner’s leitmotif technique to build a fanfare that still defines the sound of cinematic adventure; next, practise listening to short extracts of the Main Title and naming the key, intervals, rhythms and orchestration you can hear within them.

practice_questions.text: Identify the key in which the Star Wars Main Title is written.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for correctly stating B flat major.

practice_questions.text: Name the rhythmic device Williams uses beneath the opening fanfare to create forward momentum.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for identifying triplet figures or triplets.

practice_questions.text: Explain how the rising fourths and fifths in the brass fanfare help create a heroic mood.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 3 marks for identifying the interval, linking it to brass instrument projection or brightness, and connecting this to the heroic or adventurous effect on the listener.

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which Korngold's film scoring style influenced Williams' Main Title.
practice_questions.marks: Award up to 2 marks per valid point, such as full orchestral forces carrying narrative weight, memorable singable themes, or rich chromatic harmony, with credit for linking directly to the Main Title.

practice_questions.text: Define the term leitmotif and explain its importance to the structure of the Star Wars score.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for an accurate definition and up to 2 further marks for explaining its role in unifying the score through recurring themes attached to characters or ideas.

practice_questions.text: State the composer and title of the orchestral work most associated with quintal harmony and ostinato that influenced Williams' darker cues.
practice_questions.marks: Award 1 mark for Gustav Holst and 1 mark for The Planets or Mars, the Bringer of War.

glossary_terms.definition: A recurring musical theme or idea associated with a particular character, place or concept, pioneered by Wagner.
A short, bold, often brass-led musical flourish used to announce something important or grand.
A rhythmic grouping of three equal notes performed in the time normally taken by two.
A short musical pattern that is repeated persistently throughout a section of music.
Harmony built from stacked intervals of a fifth rather than the more common thirds.
A bright major key that sits comfortably within the natural range of brass instruments, giving a resonant, confident tone.
A large ensemble combining strings, woodwind, brass and percussion sections, capable of great range and power.
Erich Wolfgang Korngold, an Austrian-born composer whose lush 1930s and 1940s Hollywood scores established the symphonic film-scoring style Williams later revived.
Gustav Holst, English composer of the orchestral suite The Planets, whose driving rhythms and quintal harmony influenced Williams' style.
Richard Wagner, nineteenth-century opera composer who pioneered the leitmotif technique later adopted by film composers.

description: This lesson explores how John Williams revived the symphonic film score in his 1977 Star Wars Main Title, examining its fanfare construction, leitmotif technique and stylistic debts to Korngold and Holst.
